header.title: QuestPulse
header.excerpt:
I initially created QuestPulse to help a friend organize an interactive scavenger hunt. Then I wondered: could this become a real business?
Find out how I developed the platform and validated market demand to decide its future!

data.overview:
QuestPulse is a real-time web platform for creating, hosting, and tracking interactive GPS scavenger hunts. Players explore cities on their phones, solve clues, and unlock waypoints as they physically reach geofenced coordinates, while organizers monitor team progress and live leaderboards from a central control room using their device.

This started as an ad-hoc tool to help a friend organize a local event, but quickly turned into a deeper exploration of two things: building robust real-time software and testing product viability. Instead of building payments blindly, I set up a fake-door experiment and ran the unit economics to see if turning it into a paid SaaS was financially worth the fixed operational overhead, leading to a deliberate data-driven pivot to keep the platform free and open.
data.content:
1. Solving a Real-World Problem for a Friend

It all started with a friend who had a logistical headache.

She had previously organized a physical scavenger hunt for a group of friends, but running it was an almost absolute nightmare. She had to stay on WhatsApp with multiple teams simultaneously, manually verifying whether photos were taken in the right spots, deciding on the fly who was allowed to move to the next stage, and calculating clues and penalties in real time. Instead of enjoying the event, she was essentially acting as a human server with zero bandwidth.

When she wanted to do something similar this summer, she asked me if I could create a tool for that purpose.

Of course I could… at least try.

The goal was simple: an intuitive web application where the organizer could set up waypoints, clues, and penalties in an editor, while players would just open a link on their phones. The browser would handle the heavy lifting: checking GPS coordinates with the Geolocation API, comparing distances and unlocking clues automatically only when players were physically within a predefined radius.

2. The Field Test

Writing code that relies on the real world is terrifying. GPS drift in narrow Italian streets, spotty 4G connections, and mobile browser quirks can easily ruin the experience.

Then came the live test. We split our group of friends into two competing teams. To keep the test authentic they had no idea I had developed the web app, they just thought we were using a cool new tool found online. I even joined one of the teams as a regular player.

To my immense relief, everything worked flawlessly:

  • The GPS geofencing unlocked the next clues precisely as we stepped into the target places and streets.

  • The hint penalty system worked as intended, forcing teams to make tactical decisions (take a hint now and lose points, or keep searching?).

  • The live sync kept the competition intense.

The race remained intense until the very end, especially since my friend disabled the live leaderboard, forcing us to race blind against an ideal ghost team that was doing everything perfectly. In the end, my team ended up winning by a fair amount of points, but more importantly: the software didn't crash once, and my friend was able to actually relax and watch the game unfold from her mobile phone, casually following both teams on the real-time GPS map while riding her bike.

3. Wait, Could I Be Rich?

At the post-game chat, while everyone was still hyped, my friend (who was in on the plan with me) casually dropped the question:

"I have a confession: I actually paid for this to organize the event. If you were me, how much would you have spent on something like this?"

Some said what I expected: around 5€ or less, but other answers completely caught me off guard:

  • A few said 10 to 20€.

  • One friend, who practically carried our winning team, said 30€.

Suddenly, the developer mindset took a back seat and the aspiring entrepreneur woke up:

Wait... people actually want to pay for this? Could this become a profitable micro-SaaS?

4. The Transformation to QuestPulse

I immediately dove into the product development rabbit hole:

  1. Rebranding: I moved away from the generic internal website name "treasure-hunt" and created QuestPulse, complete with a cohesive design system, custom brand assets, and dark/light mode toggles.

  2. SaaS Experience: I designed a cool landing page with full bilingual localization (IT/EN) for international events and tourists, an interactive feature matrix, and plan tiers ranging from single-event passes (7.90€) to subscriptions for tour guides and corporate facilitators (79€–349€/year).

  3. Putting Theory into Practice: The Fake-Door Experiment

Some years ago, I was gratful to attended an inspiring workshop hosted by Google Developer Group (GDG) Milano where they broke down the concept of Fake-Door testing: validating real market demand before writing a single line of checkout code or dealing with legal overhead.

Instead of rushing to integrate Stripe, I implemented that exact framework. When a visitor clicked to purchase a plan, the app intercepted the event via custom database telemetry, recorded purchase intent, and smoothly routed them to a "Founder Waitlist" screen with an exclusive early-bird reservation.

Everything was polished. The landing page was live. I even started writing automated lead-generation scripts in Node.js to prospect local tour guides and event planners.

5. The Cold Math of Unit Economics

Then came the moment that changed the project’s direction: I sat down and did the actual math.

In Italy, launching a commercial venture isn't free. Opening and maintaining a registered sole proprietorship (“Partita IVA” or VAT number) carries roughly €3,000/year in unavoidable fixed costs, if you already apply the 35% reduction to INPS fixed contributions.

Then came the moment that changed the project’s direction: I sat down and did the actual math.

In Italy, launching a commercial venture isn't free. Opening and maintaining a registered sole proprietorship (VAT number ”Partita IVA” in the flat-tax regime) carries roughly 3,000€/year in unavoidable fixed overhead, even when applying the 35% INPS contribution reduction for merchants, plus accountant fees and mandatory chamber of commerce dues, completely independent of whether you make a single sale.

I opened a spreadsheet to run the break-even numbers:

  • The Goal: Cover the 3,000€/year fixed baseline just to avoid losing money.

  • The Product: A tour guide license priced at 79€/year.

  • The Math: To break even after payment gateway fees, I needed at least 42 paying customers for the first year.

Then I looked at realistic acquisition channels. Selling a 79€ product through manual outbound (cold emails, DMs on Instagram, direct outreach) typically converts at around 1.5% to 2% in best-case B2B scenarios.

I would have had to manually hunt, qualify, and message over 2,000 people just to make €0 in net profit.

It is simply not sustainable to run a high-touch outbound sales process from scratch for a product priced under €100. Low-cost tools require massive organic inbound traffic or viral word-of-mouth, things that take months or years to build. Outbound sales only really make sense for high-ticket contracts (€1,000+), but I refused to go down that road: I had no intention of charging people exorbitant prices for software that costs me virtually nothing to host and run.

6. Removing the Paywall (for now)

A lot of founders fall in love with their ideas and burn thousands of euros on taxes and bureaucracy before accepting market reality.

Instead of stubbornly pushing through or taking on financial risk at the wrong stage, I made a pragmatic decision: I pulled the plug on premature monetization.

I rolled back the database migrations, stripped the fake-door telemetry, deleted the paywalls, and restored the full feature set as a 100% free and open platform.

Now, anyone can log in, create complex multi-team scavenger hunts, monitor participants on a live map, and use the full feature set without spending a single cent. The only planned feature I intentionally postponed, because it would incur real ongoing infrastructure costs for storage and CDN bandwidth, was photo challenges where teams upload pictures/selfies and organizers verify them on the fly.

Does this mean the commercial door is closed forever? Not at all.

It just means I chose another sequence: Product-Led Growth first, monetization later. If low-ticket tools need organic volume and word-of-mouth to survive, keeping QuestPulse open and free is the fastest way to get it into the hands of hundreds of event hosts, schools, and friends. Once a solid user base is established and organic demand warrants it, introducing paid infrastructure tiers (like photo quests or custom branding) will be a natural evolution built on actual traffic rather than cold calls.

7. What This Project Taught Me

QuestPulse is easily one of the most rewarding projects I’ve built, not because it made me rich, but because of what it taught me across the entire product lifecycle:

1. Code is only 20% of the battle: Building a real-time GPS app with Supabase Realtime, Leaflet, and Next.js is challenging, but making it financially sustainable is a completely different skill.

2. Test before you commit: Applying the Fake-Door concepts learned at GDG Milano and running unit economics early saved me thousands of euros and endless administrative headaches.

3. Patience is a strategy: Choosing to grow an open product rather than forcing an unsustainable sales model is often the smartest business move you can make.

Today QuestPulse exists as a battle-tested, production-ready platform that solved a real headache for a friend, and gave me the best hands-on masterclass in full-stack engineering and product strategy I could have asked for.
